system: You are a writer of plain, descriptive encyclopaedia-style prose.
message: Write about 2210 words on the natural and settlement history of a fictional river valley, the Aldern, from its geology to its villages, mills and bridges. This is part 3 of 4 of one continuous article; write only this part, continuing the account in order (part 1 begins at the valley's geology; part 4 ends with the present day). Write descriptive prose only: what things are, where, when, how they work physically, how they changed over time. Do NOT discuss evidence, research methods, how to reason, how to judge claims, reviewing, teamwork, collaboration, decision-making, advice, or controversies and debates. No lists, no headings beyond a title, no questions to the reader. Invent a fictional place where needed; do not cite studies or numbers from studies.

# The Aldern Valley: Mills, Bridges and the Working River

By the close of the thirteenth century the villages of the Aldern had settled into the places they would keep for the next five hundred years. Hollin Cross stood on its gravel terrace above the upper gorge, Wethercombe spread along the spring line at the foot of the western scarp, and Saltry, the largest of the valley settlements, sat where the river slackened and widened before entering the clay vale. Between and around them the river itself began to change. It was no longer only a boundary, a fishing water and a source of flood. It became a source of power, and over the following centuries the Aldern was harnessed, divided, embanked and crossed until much of its course was as much a made thing as a natural one.

The first mills on the Aldern were small undershot wheels set directly into the current. They stood at points where the channel narrowed between rock outcrops, so that the water ran fast without the need for much construction. The earliest of them, below Hollin Cross, was a timber building on a stone footing, with a wheel of oak paddles turning in a slot cut partly into the limestone of the riverbed. The wheel drove a single pair of stones through a horizontal shaft and a cog-and-rung gear, grinding barley and oats for the upland farms. Such mills turned slowly and stopped altogether in dry summers, when the upper river shrank to a chain of pools linked by a trickle over the bedrock. In winter they were at the mercy of floods that carried trees and ice down the gorge, and the Hollin Cross mill was rebuilt at least three times on the same footing before the end of the fourteenth century.

Lower in the valley the gradient was gentler and the river too broad and slow to turn a wheel unaided. Here the millwrights built weirs. A weir on the Aldern was at first a line of driven timber stakes set across the channel at a slant, the gaps packed with brushwood, stones and clay. Behind it the water rose into a millpond that stretched upstream for some distance, drowning the shallows and turning a stretch of braided gravel channels into a single still reach. From the side of the pond a leat, a narrow artificial channel, carried water along the valley side at a slightly lower gradient than the river, so that by the time it reached the mill it stood several feet above the natural bed. This difference in height, the head, was what drove the wheel. Water passing through the mill fell back into the river by a tailrace, rejoining the main channel some way downstream.

The Saltry mill, built on this pattern, became the principal corn mill of the lower valley. Its leat left the river above the village, ran behind the churchyard and the backs of the street houses, and passed beneath the road in a stone culvert before reaching the mill building at the eastern edge of the settlement. The mill held two pairs of stones, one of local gritstone quarried from the eastern hills for coarse grinding and one of imported burr stone for finer flour. Its breastshot wheel received water at about the height of its axle, so that the weight of the water in the buckets as well as its movement turned the wheel. This was more efficient than the undershot wheels of the upper valley and allowed the Saltry mill to work through all but the driest weeks of the year.

The weirs had effects well beyond the mills. Each one held back sediment as well as water, and the ponds behind them slowly filled with silt and sand washed down from the ploughed slopes above. Within a few generations the reach above the Saltry weir had become shallow and marshy at its edges, with beds of reed and sedge spreading from the banks. Eels gathered in the slack water and in the leats, and eel traps of woven willow became a fixture of every mill. Fish that had once moved freely up the river to spawn on the gravels below Hollin Cross found their way barred, and the runs of sea trout that had come up the Aldern in autumn dwindled through the later medieval centuries. The river below each weir, robbed of its sediment, cut down into its bed, so that the channel became deeper and the banks steeper downstream of the mills than above them.

The floodplain itself changed in response. Meadows along the lower Aldern had always been wet in winter, but the raised water levels behind the weirs kept them wet for longer. The farmers of Saltry and Wethercombe turned this to use. From the sixteenth century onward they cut networks of shallow channels across the meadows, fed by sluices from the river or the leats. In late winter they let water flow thinly over the grass, a practice known locally as floating. The moving water kept frost from the ground and carried a fine film of silt onto the turf, so that the grass began to grow several weeks earlier than on unwatered land. The meadows were then drained, grazed by ewes and lambs in spring, and closed for hay in summer. The pattern of ridges and channels made by this work still shows across the lower floodplain as low parallel banks in the turf, most clearly when the grass is short or when floodwater lies in the old furrows.

Mills multiplied along the Aldern through the sixteenth and seventeenth centuries. Fulling mills appeared on the middle river, where cloth woven in the cottages of Wethercombe and the scarp-foot hamlets was brought to be cleansed and thickened. A fulling mill used its wheel to lift heavy wooden hammers, known as stocks, which fell repeatedly on the wet cloth lying in a trough with water and fuller's earth. The pounding matted the woollen fibres together, shrinking and strengthening the cloth. After fulling the cloth was stretched on tenter frames in fields beside the mill to dry, and the meadows below Wethercombe were for a time lined with rows of these frames, each length of cloth held taut by hooks along its edges. Downstream of the fulling mills the river ran grey and soapy, and the fuller's earth, a pale clay dug from a pit on the eastern hills, settled in the pools.

On the tributary streams that came down from the western scarp, smaller mills were built for other purposes. The Kell Brook, which falls steeply through a wooded combe above Wethercombe, carried a string of three mills within the space of a mile, each taking its water from the tailrace of the one above. The highest was a bark mill, crushing oak bark for the tanneries of Saltry. The middle mill ground flint and bone for the potteries and for fertiliser. The lowest was a small paper mill, which pulped linen rags in water and laid the pulp in thin sheets on wire moulds. The steep fall of the brook allowed these mills to use overshot wheels, in which water was carried by a wooden trough to the top of the wheel and dropped into the buckets, turning the wheel by weight alone. Overshot wheels needed far less water than undershot ones, which suited the small and flashy streams of the scarp.

Crossing the Aldern had always been a matter of fords. The river in its natural state was wide and shallow over much of its lower course, and there were several places where gravel bars ran nearly across the channel. The main ford at Saltry lay a little upstream of the later bridge, on a bar of coarse gravel that carried the road from the clay vale up into the valley. Carts crossed here at low water; at high water travellers waited, sometimes for days. Footbridges of timber planks laid on trestles served those on foot in the villages, but they were swept away in most floods and had to be replaced every few years.

The construction of the weirs made fords more difficult, since the raised water drowned the gravel bars and deepened the channels below. The first permanent bridge over the Aldern was built at Saltry in the late fifteenth century. It was a stone bridge of four arches, built of the same limestone as the church, each arch a pointed form springing from piers that stood on the riverbed. The piers were shaped on their upstream faces into triangular cutwaters, which split the current and turned aside floating debris. Above the cutwaters, the parapet was carried out into small triangular refuges where people on foot could step aside from passing carts. The roadway was narrow, wide enough for a single wagon, and humped over the arches so that the bridge rose noticeably from each bank to its centre.

The Saltry bridge changed the way the lower valley was used. The road through the village became a through route between the clay vale and the upland, and inns and smithies grew up along it. A small market was held on the open ground at the eastern end of the bridge, where the road widened. The bridge also changed the river. Its piers narrowed the channel, so that in flood the water backed up behind it and spread across the meadows upstream, while immediately below the bridge the current scoured deep holes in the bed. One of these pools, below the second arch, remained the deepest point on the lower Aldern for centuries and was used by the village as a washing place and, in hot summers, for bathing.

Upstream, the crossing at Hollin Cross was made by a single high arch of rubble stone, built over the narrowest point of the gorge where the river ran between limestone walls. Because the rock on either side provided natural abutments, no piers were needed in the water, and the bridge stood above the reach of all but the greatest floods. It was a packhorse bridge, with low parapets that allowed laden horses to pass without catching their panniers, and it carried a track that ran over the eastern hills to the lead workings beyond. Strings of ponies crossed it in summer carrying ore and returned with grain and salt.

Between these two crossings the middle valley remained bridgeless for longer. At Wethercombe the river was crossed by a ford and a ferry, the ferry being a flat-bottomed boat drawn across on a rope stretched between two posts. The ferry house stood on the western bank, a small stone building with a single room and a fireplace, and the ferryman kept a lantern at the window so that travellers could find the crossing after dark. A timber bridge was finally built at Wethercombe in the early eighteenth century, resting on oak piles driven into the gravel and braced with diagonal timbers. It was replaced in stone about sixty years later after the piles had been loosened by repeated floods.

The eighteenth century brought the most intensive use of the river. Corn milling expanded to serve a growing population, and several of the older mills were rebuilt in brick with larger wheels and additional pairs of stones. The Saltry mill was raised to three storeys, with a sack hoist under a projecting gable lifting grain to the top floor, from which it was fed down through the building by gravity, passing through the stones, the dressing machines and the bagging floor in turn. Its timber weir was replaced with one of dressed stone, built in a long curve across the river with a sloping face over which the water slid in a smooth sheet. A fish pass of stepped pools was built into one side, although it was too steep for most fish to climb.

At the same time, the lower Aldern was straightened and embanked for navigation. Below Saltry the river had wandered across its floodplain in broad loops, and these were cut through by new channels that shortened its course by more than a mile. The old loops, left without a through flow, silted at their ends and became still backwaters, which slowly filled with reeds and alder and turned to wet woodland. Earth banks were raised along the new channel to hold floods back from the fields, and a towpath ran along the top of the northern bank. Shallow-draught barges were hauled by horses from the vale as far as a wharf below the Saltry bridge, carrying coal, lime and timber up the valley and taking grain, cloth and tanned hides down. A pound lock beside the Saltry weir allowed barges to pass the fall, its two pairs of timber gates enclosing a chamber of stone that filled and emptied through sluices in the gates.

The navigation, the mills and the floating meadows all depended on the same water, and the river was divided among them by a growing system of sluices, hatches and side channels. In wet seasons there was water enough for all, but in dry summers the leats drew off so much of the flow that the main channel between the weir and the tailrace dwindled to a narrow stream, leaving long reaches of gravel and weed exposed. In these reaches the water warmed in the sun and grew thick with green algae, and the river below Saltry in late summer carried a distinct smell of mud and weed.

By the close of the eighteenth century the Aldern from Hollin Cross to the vale was a sequence of managed reaches, each held up by a weir and drained by a mill, joined by straightened channels and crossed by a handful of stone bridges. The valley floor was patterned with water meadows, tenter fields, osier beds and old river loops. The river still flooded in winter and still shrank in summer, but the shape of its floods and the pattern of its flow were now set as much by stone and timber as by rain and rock.
